peer_review_rounds.author_response: Author reply: We sincerely thank the editor and the reviewers for their time and professional comments during the review process. We benefited a lot from the reviewers’ comments and carefully revised the manuscript in accordance with the comments. In particular, we are grateful to Reviewer 2 and Reviewer 3 for their affirmation of our research at the end of the previous review and their willingness to accept it. This has provided great encouragement for our work. In this revision, we provide a point‑by‑point response to Reviewer 1’s comments below and detail the corresponding changes made to the manuscript. Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): This revision partially clarified the previous queries. Some key concerns remain. Most of them are critically linked with the justification of physical-chemical performance. Author reply: We sincerely thank Reviewer 1 for the valuable and constructive feedback, which has greatly contributed to improving the quality of our manuscript. Some critical concerns are: Comment 1: The multi-length-scale design and phase transformation seems be lack of justification, most of them are based on the illustration and/or with the indirect assessment. I was wondering if there are any possible in-situ measurement to quantify the interaction forces/effects? The response on the porous structure should be distinguished with further mechanic analysis on non-linear regime such as a hyper-elasticity, poroelasticity, etc. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. To address the concerns regarding the lack of direct evidence for the multi-scale design, the absence of in-situ measurement, and the insufficient analysis of nonlinear mechanics, we have made the following additions and clarifications. In addition to the existing micro-CT three-dimensional reconstruction, we have incorporated localized in-situ scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations, which capture the real-time microstructural deformation and contact evolution of TEPUF during compression. Multi-scale design: At the nanoscale, hydrogen bonds between the sulfonic acid groups in PEDOT:PSS and the -NH groups in WPU enhance interfacial adhesion, as evidenced by the absence of coating delamination after 20,000 compression cycles (Fig. 2h in the Revised Manuscript), with negligible changes in resistance and Seebeck coefficient, thereby preserving conductive pathways. At the microscale, the SWCNT/PEDOT:PSS layer conformally envelops the PUF struts, as visualized in SEM cross-sections (Fig. S4 in the revised Supporting Information), ensuring uniform conductivity without aggregation. This is corroborated by stable electrical output under humidity variations (Fig. 2d in the Revised Manuscript). At the macroscale, the open-cell porosity establishes isolated air pockets, yielding the observed ultralow thermal conductivity (~0.0445 W m−1 K−1, Fig. S2 in the revised Supporting Information) and enabling precise thermal sensing (0.05 K resolution, Fig. 2e in the Revised Manuscript). These scales synergistically confer hydrophobicity (contact angle 112°, Fig. 2b in the Revised Manuscript) and breathability (406 mm s−1, Fig. 2c in the Revised Manuscript), arising from the interplay of intramolecular cohesion, surface uniformity, and void architecture, rather than isolated attributes. In-situ SEM imaging demonstrates that, during the initial phase of applied compressive loading, the foam struts exhibit coherent elastic buckling and minor deformation, with the toroidal cell walls undergoing mutual compression while maintaining overall continuity (Fig. R1). Stress is uniformly diffusion across the toroidal walls and scaffold network, thereby preventing unstable buckling. This dissipation mechanism validates the multi-scale architecture’s ability to sustain macroscopic external loads while accommodating microscopic stress relief through the coordinated deformation of the compliant struts. In conjunction with stress-strain curves and metrics such as energy dissipation and elastic recovery ratio, these observations confirm the pronounced nonlinear hyperelastic character of TEPUF (Fig. R2, Fig. R3 and Fig. R4). Specifically, the stress-strain response exhibits marked nonlinearity, with low hysteresis loss and high elastic rebound during cyclic compression hallmarks of hyper-elasticity. In contrast, canonical porous elastomers often display substantial viscoelastic dissipation and time-dependence, neither of which is evident here. Thus, the mechanical response of TEPUF is dominated by the elastic recoil of the solid scaffold, rather than poroelastic effects governed by internal fluid flow within the pores. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Page 12, with changes highlighted in blue. Comment 2: It is interesting that the authors provided the FEA results of the potential and stress distribution of the TEPUF under different temperature difference (ΔTs) and pressures in Figure R5. However, this figure brought a lot unclarity in the data with different temperature difference (ΔTs). The simulation should benchmark the temperature with different magnitudes, as the response could be different within each range. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. To clarify the thermoelectric behavior under different temperature differences (ΔTs) and directly address the concern that device responses might vary across temperature intervals, we performed supplementary finite-element analyses (FEA) over a broadened ΔT range. Guided by the reviewer’s suggestion, we systematically benchmarked sensor behavior across multiple ΔT magnitudes, from ultra-small to comparatively large, under two representative compressive strains (20% and 60%). Simulation set-up and ΔT ranges: At fixed compressive strains of 20% and 60%, we prescribed ΔT at three levels to probe potential thermo-mechanical coupling. Small ΔTs: 0.05 K, 0.1 K (ultra-fine temperature resolution). Medium ΔTs: 1 K, 3 K, 5 K (typical operating window). Large ΔTs: 20 K, 40 K, 60 K (pronounced thermal gradients). For each condition, the specified ΔT was applied at the given strain to evaluate whether responses differ across temperature intervals. Results: Benchmarking across ΔT magnitudes demonstrates robust decoupling between the thermal-electrical and mechanical channels, thereby addressing the reviewer’s concern. Measurable thermovoltages are obtained even at ultra-small ΔTs (0.05K, 0.1K) and are independent of the applied mechanical load (Fig. R5). The device reliably detects minute temperature changes without pressure-induced artifacts. Within this common working range (1K, 3K, 5K), thermo-mechanical decoupling remains stable (Fig. R6). Even under high thermal gradients (20K, 40K, 60K), the imposed pressure exerts a negligible influence on the thermoelectric output (Fig. R7). Across all ΔT levels, the thermal-electrical pathway and the mechanical response remain decoupled, with no observable cross-talk between thermoelectric output and strain-induced effects. The observed decoupling originates from the architecture and materials design of the polyurethane foam with conductive fillers (TEPUF). Under compression, cell walls deform without catastrophic collapse, preserving the integrity of internal temperature-gradient pathways. Mechanical deformation is primarily accommodated by the skeleton and contact points, effectively isolating the heat-conduction routes from mechanical perturbations. Consequently, applied pressure does not materially alter the temperature field and thus does not affect the thermovoltage, the device sustains a stable ΔT under compression. In parallel, the piezoresistive network is governed by strain-driven contact evolution and, within the investigated range, is insensitive to temperature variations. This structural feature underpins the consistent decoupling observed at every ΔT magnitude and confirms independent dual-parameter sensing over a broad operating envelope. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Page 14 and the Supporting Information on Pages 39, 40, and 41, with changes highlighted in blue. Comment 3: The testing data obtained from deploying the device in an inhaling mask, has a lot unclarity, the date in Fig 4 a-b, with minor fluctuations on output from temperature change of a few degrees is not convincing. The static charge could cause more fluctuation! Has the device been grounded properly? This should have a detailed schematic illustration for the testing setting. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. We address the reviewer’s concerns point by point regarding the lack of clarity in the data presented in Fig. 4a-b, the unconvincing nature of the small fluctuations in output resulting from temperature changes of a few degrees, the potential for greater fluctuations due to static charge, the proper grounding of the device, and the need for a detailed schematic of the testing setup. To clarify the perceived lack of clarity in the testing data and the unconvincing small fluctuations in output, these data derive from real underwater respiratory monitoring experiments, in which TEPUF is integrated into a face mask and directly responds to the temperature gradient (ΔT) and mechanical perturbations from exhaled airflow. Fig. 4a provides a schematic of the underwater temperature sensing mechanism, while Fig. 4b illustrates changes in voltage (V) and resistance (R) during long-term respiratory monitoring, with the fluctuations reflecting authentic physiological signals rather than noise. Specifically, respiratory cycles induce ΔT variations typically ranging from 0.5 to 5 K (with exhaled air warmer than the ambient environment), yielding thermoelectric voltage fluctuations of ~0.17 to 1.72 mV, this correspondence is consistent with the thermoelectric devices in other studies 1-3. Such small fluctuations are expected given the modest ΔT in human respiration, but our device’s resolution of 0.05 K (Fig. 2e in the Revised Manuscript) enables their reliable detection. Regarding the possibility of greater fluctuations due to static charge, we agree that static charge could potentially affect sensor performance in a flexible system. To verify this, we used an electrometer to measure the device’s static voltage before and after grounding, showing that grounding reduces static voltage to zero (Fig. R8). We repeated the respiratory monitoring experiments under conditions with and without static charge (including normal breathing, deep breathing, rapid breathing, and nose breathing), and the results indicate that the voltage outputs for the same respiratory intensity are nearly identical. This confirms that static charge has a negligible impact and that the data in Fig. 4b are not influenced by static charge. With respect to proper grounding of the device, we confirm that all experiments were conducted with appropriate grounding, the TEPUF array is connected via copper electrodes and silver paste and linked to a Keithley 2450 source meter (which includes built-in grounding functionality). The device’s substrate is grounded via copper wires. For the detailed schematic of the testing setup, we agree this is a valuable addition to improve reproducibility. We have included a new schematic illustrating the face mask deployment, including the TEPUF integration position, grounding configuration, and data acquisition system (Fig. R9). Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Page 16 and the Supporting Information on Page 46, with changes highlighted in blue. Comment 4: In Table R1, the comparison shown amazing advantage of the proposed technology. However, this level of precision needs a very critical testing environment to do the experiment, such as clean room. I am not persuaded by the method part as described in this work. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. To address the potential impact of environmental factors on testing precision, we conducted multiple independent replicate experiments in both a super clean bench (temperature 25°C, relative humidity 60%) and a standard laboratory environment (temperature 25°C, relative humidity 60%), comparing the device’s temperature resolution and strain response time. The results show consistent data across both environments: the minimum temperature resolution is approximately 0.05 K, and the compression response time is approximately 40 ms, with differences within the error range (Fig. R10 and Fig. R11). Additionally, we performed standard deviation statistics on the measurement data, finding that environmental changes have minimal impact on output signal fluctuations. Therefore, we conclude that the superior detection precision arises from the material design itself, rather than relying on stringent clean room conditions. To further demonstrate the validity of the methods and elucidate the scientific principles and innovations underlying the superior performance, we note that the benchmark studies in Table R1 similarly report high-precision metrics (ΔT responses of 0.2-1 K and strain times of 130-510 ms) using standard laboratory methods without clean rooms. Gao et al. used simple dip-coating of melamine sponge with PEDOT:PSS/CNTs, followed by drying under ambient conditions and testing with a Keithley meter in a regular lab setup, achieving a minimum temperature response of ~0.4 K 4. He et al. dispersed CNT ink with chitin nanocrystals via sonication and screen-printed it, with measurements in a standard environment, reporting a minimum ΔT response of ~0.7 K 5. He et al. prepared waste cotton-derived aerogels through sustainable mixing and freeze-drying, tested in typical lab conditions, with minimum temperature responses around ~0.27 K 6. Fu et al. employed roll-to-roll fabrication of chalcogenide glass-polymer films, with sensor tests in ambient labs, achieving ~0.2 K resolution 7. Cui et al. coated fabrics with PEDOT/MWCNTs via immersion and hot-air cross-linking, evaluated in standard setups, with minimum ΔT responses of ~1 K 8. These references consistently demonstrate that high-precision thermoelectric and strain sensing in similar devices can be reliably achieved without clean rooms. Furthermore, from a mechanistic perspective, the achievement of 0.05 K level temperature resolution primarily stems from the synergistic interplay between the three-dimensional open-cell foam structure and the flexible conductive framework. The ultralow thermal conductivity (~0.0445 W m−1 K−1) arises from the high porosity (~97%) 3D porous structure, creating numerous internal static air pockets that minimize thermal diffusion and enable detection of minute temperature gradients. For the rapid compression rebound (40 ms response time), the scientific principle lies in the material’s nonlinear mechanical regime: the hyperelastic behavior of the PUF framework facilitates rapid recovery through structural reconfiguration (pore wall bending rather than collapse), while the waterproof coating enhances durability under repeated cycles (Fig. 2h in the Revised Manuscript). This innovation addresses the trade-off between elasticity and conductivity in flexible sensors, enabling real-time multi-modal decoupling (temperature-strain) in high-humidity settings, surpassing reported response times, and advancing wearable electronics for marine exploration. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Page 22, with changes highlighted in blue. Comment 5: In the simulation results from Figure 3f, there are substantial deviation of the output (in m-Volts) with 50% deformation and 12 degreeC temperature variation. However, the actual change (micro-Volts) is far more less than the condition, I don’t think this is a proper theoretical-experimental validation as the conditions have magnitude gap between each. I can not say that the methods are robust, and results are rigour. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. The reviewer noted that in the simulation results of Fig. 3f in the original manuscript, applying 50% compressive strain and a 12 °C temperature change yielded voltage outputs on the milli-volts (mV) scale, while the actual experimental signal changes are on the micro-volt (μV) scale, indicating a significant gap in the magnitude of the stimulus conditions. Thus, the reviewer questions whether the mismatch between the original simulation and experimental validation conditions may undermine the validity of the result comparison. The FEA simulations in Fig. 3f are intended to illustrate the decoupling mechanism between mechanical strain and thermoelectric potential, rather than to provide an exact quantitative match for specific experimental conditions. These simulations employ a multi-physics approach (coupling solid mechanics, electric currents, and heat transfer modules in COMSOL, as detailed in Eqs. S1-S12 of the Supporting Information) to demonstrate that external pressure has minimal impact on the thermoelectric potential distribution, even under substantial deformation (50% strain) and temperature gradients (ΔT = 12 K). This qualitative and trend-based validation is a standard practice in thermoelectric sensor research, where FEA is often used to predict stress and potential fields under controlled conditions to highlight underlying physics, without accounting for experimental-specific influences. To address this concern, we have made the following improvements in the latest revision. We have added experimental data for thermo-mechanical decoupling at the μV level. As shown in Fig. R12, under 50% deformation, different small temperature differences were applied. Even at weak signals on the μV scale, the two outputs maintain clear separation characteristics. Additionally, the device exhibits dynamic decoupling capability. At low temperature difference magnitudes, multiple experiments still show highly reproducible response curves, demonstrating that the device’s thermoelectric and piezoresistive signals can still be reliably distinguished and stably measured under weak stimulus conditions. We have conducted finite element simulations based on parameters fully consistent with the experiments (Fig. R13). Voltage distributions were calculated under compression strain consistent with the experiments (50%) and different temperature differences, with results showing outputs consistent with experiments, both at the μV level, and spatial distribution trends aligning. This further verifies the effectiveness of our theoretical model under weak signals, indicating that the model can accurately predict the impact of small thermoelectric and piezoresistive changes on output signals. Through the above supplementary experiments and simulation results, we find that theoretical predictions and actual measurements are highly consistent in both signal magnitude and change trends. This effectively addresses the reviewer’s question regarding the previously high simulation output, eliminating the mismatch in comparisons under different magnitudes. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions, which guided these targeted additions and enhanced the rigor of our methods and results. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Page 15 and the Supporting Information on Pages 42 and 43, with changes highlighted in blue. Comment 6: The underwater part is particularly tricky, I would recommend author to check the Professor Wanlin Guo’s work in NUAA, to understand the ‘Hydrovoltaic energy from water’, then justify the influencing factor properly. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. As noted by the reviewer, we recognize the potential complexities in the underwater section of our manuscript, particularly the influence of hydrovoltaic effects at water-solid interfaces. Following your recommendation, we have carefully reviewed the pioneering work of Professor Wanlin Guo’s group at NUAA on ‘Hydrovoltaic energy from water’ and conducted an in-depth analysis of hydrovoltaic effects and their key influencing factors based on the literature. The hydrovoltaic effect refers to the generation of electricity through interactions at water-solid interfaces. When nanomaterial surfaces come into contact with flowing water, evaporating water molecules, moisture or ions in solution during dynamic processes, charge rearrangement, electric double-layer changes, or even potential generation may occur at the interface, leading to additional voltage output 9-16. These phenomena could interfere with the thermoelectric signals we intend to measure. After a thorough examination of Professor Guo’s group’s research, we gained important insights: their studies systematically summarize the mechanisms of dynamic energy harvesting from water flow, waves, natural evaporation, and moisture adsorption. These works highlight the tremendous potential of hydrovoltaic effects while reminding us that in underwater or high-humidity thermoelectric monitoring, factors such as charge transfer at water-solid interfaces and ionic concentrations must be carefully evaluated to avoid signal crosstalk. To verify whether our device would be affected by the hydrovoltaic effect and allay the reviewer’s concerns in this regard, we focused on the core influencing factors of the hydrovoltaic effect proposed by Professor Guo’s research group (water flow, evaporation, water adsorption, droplet movement, ion concentration), combined with the actual application scenarios of our materials (underwater physiological monitoring and high-humidity environments, such as breathing, body temperature and motion signal collection). Water flow: Fix the TEPUF sample in an underwater environment, use a peristaltic pump to control the water flow rate (~1 m/s) while maintaining no ΔT conditions, and measure its output voltage. Compare the voltage output under still water conditions (flow rate 0 m/s) with that under water flow conditions to evaluate the influence brought by water flow. Water evaporation: First, soak the TEPUF sample in deionized water for 30 minutes to allow it to fully absorb water (simulating long-term underwater contact). Then transfer the sample to a laboratory environment (temperature 25°C, relative humidity 60%) and continuously monitor the output voltage under no ΔT conditions for 10 minutes to examine the influence caused by evaporation. Moisture adsorption: Place the TEPUF in a constant temperature and humidity chamber and simulate different moisture levels by changing the relative humidity (from 40% to 90%). Maintain no ΔT conditions and continuously measure the sample’s terminal voltage to assess the contribution of moisture adsorption to the output signal. Droplet impact: Simulate water droplet motion under underwater conditions: Use a syringe to precisely release a single water droplet (volume approximately 0.1 mL, falling freely from 10 cm above the sample) to impact the TEPUF surface, and record the transient voltage changes. This experiment can detect whether the kinetic energy of the water droplet interacting with the sample interface generates potential. Ionic concentration: Soak the TEPUF in seawater. Measure the terminal voltage and resistance value of the TEPUF under no ΔT to compare the influence of seawater on voltage and resistance output. The above experiments involve major factors (such as water flow, evaporation, humidity, charge/ion movement) derived from the core influencing factors proposed by Professor Guo’s group. Our purpose is to simulate possible water environmental changes in actual monitoring scenarios and verify their impact on thermoelectric signals. The experimental results show under all test conditions, whether still or dynamic water flow, different humidity, single droplet impact, or seawater, the output voltage of the TEPUF samples is close to baseline levels, with no significant additional potential generation detected (Fig. R14, Fig. R15, Fig. R16, Fig. R17 and Fig. R18). This is also attributed to our material design. We employed a composite waterproof coating of SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS/WPU, whose hydrogen-bonded network inhibits water permeation, as shown in the supporting information, with a surface water contact angle of approximately 112° and no significant performance degradation in long-term immersion tests. This design minimizes the possibility of water penetrating the sensitive film, thereby reducing the impact of hydrovoltaic effects on thermoelectric signal measurements, ensuring that the measured voltage primarily originates from thermoelectric effects rather than hydrovoltaic effect. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Page 19 and the Supporting Information on Pages 58, 59, 60, 61 and 62, with changes highlighted in blue.

peer_review_rounds.author_response: Author reply: We sincerely thank Reviewer 1 for the valuable and constructive feedback, which has significantly improved the quality of our manuscript. We also appreciate the reviewer’s acknowledgment of the enhanced clarity and logical coherence resulting from the new data. To address the concerns regarding the specific working mechanism, underlying scientific interpretation, and structure–property relationships, we have made substantial revisions. In particular, we have incorporated additional two-dimensional (2D) simulations to provide deeper analysis and clearer explanations in the revised manuscript. Specific working mechanism: We have clarified the specific working mechanism of the TEPUF in the revised manuscript. The device operates by generating two distinct electrical signals in response to thermal and mechanical stimuli, enabled by a dual-mode thermoelectric–piezoresistive design. A temperature gradient induces a thermal voltage determined by the Seebeck coefficient of the SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS network, whereas external pressure or strain alters the resistance of the intrinsic conductive framework through the piezoresistive effect. These two outputs are intrinsically decoupled and recorded on separate channels, ensuring the absence of cross-talk between thermal and mechanical responses. The material composition and structural design are purposefully engineered to achieve this decoupling: the incorporation of SWCNTs into the PEDOT:PSS polymer simultaneously enhances electrical conductivity and thermopower, while the hyperelastic three-dimensional (3D) porous WPU foam functions as a thermally insulating, mechanically compliant scaffold that minimizes mutual interference between heat and stress stimuli. Scientific principles: Our thermoelectric device produces a voltage signal in response to temperature differences and a resistance signal in response to mechanical deformation, inherently separating the two stimuli without requiring complex decoupling algorithms. The thermoelectric output arises from charge-carrier diffusion within the SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS composite, generating an open-circuit voltage described by V = S × ΔT. In parallel, the piezoresistive response originates from the conductive SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS network embedded within the elastic WPU matrix: when compressed, the network density increases while the contact resistance decreases, yielding a distinct resistance change. We further highlight that the device’s underwater and high-strain performance is supported by well-established physical principles. The porous foam and waterproof WPU architecture prevent water ingress and help maintain a stable temperature gradient, while the robust SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS/WPU composite network preserves electrical conductivity during repeated deformation. As added validation, we now provide experimental results demonstrating that the TEPUF maintains stable thermoelectric output and piezoresistive response over thousands of cycles and during submersion, confirming that the underlying physics of our design remain reliable under practical operating conditions. Structure-property relationship: The material composition (SWCNTs, PEDOT:PSS, and WPU) together with the foam’s microcellular architecture creates a synergistic structure–property relationship that enables dual-mode sensing with high sensitivity and elasticity. In the revision, we have adopted a multilengthscale approach and complemented it with 2D finite-element simulations to more rigorously interpret the underlying mechanisms (see detailed analysis in Response to Comment 1). Our modification to the manuscript: In response to the reviewer’s comments regarding the specific working mechanism, underlying scientific principles, and structure–property relationships, we have made targeted revisions to the Conclusion section. We have also added a final statement summarizing the multilengthscale approach and the 2D finite-element simulations. These revisions have been incorporated on Pages 20–21, with all changes highlighted in blue. The following things need be also cleared up: 1. In my comment 1, the concern is about the justification of the change of the porous and the clearance of dynamic of change. While the author offer a variety on the degree, but this is not the typical identification by the homogeneity and degree of deformation. Also the discussion of porosity should consider the local deformation. A multilengthscale approach will offer more academic value on the work. Sadly to say that, all above is missing at current manuscript. I guess a planar simulation in 2D would help. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To address the concern, we conducted a 2D finite-element simulation of the foam cross-section under compression and performed a multilengthscale approach to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. As the compressive strain increases, the foam’s initially open cells deform into progressively flatter shapes. The 2D model clearly shows pore walls moving closer together and eventually pressing against one another under load, transitioning from an open-cell geometry to a flattened-cell structure at higher strains (Fig. R1). This behavior is consistent with our experimental observations, where the cell walls gradually flatten and form broader contact interfaces as the foam is compressed. With increasing compressive strain, the pore size steadily decreases. The simulation shows a continuous reduction in pore volume from low to high strain, indicating that the porosity diminishes gradually rather than abruptly. This behavior reflects a uniform deformation of the porous network. As the pores flatten and the pore walls bend, the structure can recover once the load is removed. The 2D simulation confirms that deformation is primarily accommodated through elastic bending of the cell walls rather than permanent collapse, an intrinsic characteristic of the foam’s hyperelastic response. Even at high strain, a porous scaffold remains, enabling the foam to return to its original shape upon unloading. This preservation of porous architecture under substantial compression directly supports the material’s excellent elastic rebound and long-term cyclic durability. In addition to the 2D mechanical stress simulations, we have expanded our analysis to include a 2D thermoelectric potential-field simulation under a temperature difference of ΔT = 12 ℃ (Fig. R2). The resulting voltage distribution remains uniform and unchanged even under large compressive strains, demonstrating that the thermoelectric output is not affected by mechanical loading. This new simulation explicitly validates the mechanical–thermal decoupling mechanism and confirms that a stable thermoelectric potential field is maintained despite applied pressure. We further strengthened the discussion by situating our findings within a multilengthscale framework. At the nanoscale, strong hydrogen bonding among SWCNTs, PEDOT:PSS, and WPU forms a robust yet reversible polymer–nanotube network that preserves electrical conductivity under strain. At the microscale, the open-cell architecture functions as an effective stress-buffering system: under compression, the pore walls deform first at their weakest points, then progressively at the junctions, and ultimately the cells compress along the vertical axis while exhibiting slight lateral expansion. At the macroscale, the interconnected foam network distributes external load uniformly, enabling the device to endure 20,000 compression cycles even under underwater conditions. In summary, the combined 2D simulation results provide spatially resolved, multiscale insights into how the foam’s porosity evolves under compression while maintaining stable signal output. These findings directly address the reviewer’s request for a detailed multiscale explanation of porosity evolution and signal robustness, demonstrating that the device’s porous architecture can undergo substantial deformation without compromising its thermoelectric performance. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Pages 15-16, 36 and Pages 44-45 in the revised Supporting Information, with changes highlighted in blue. 2. In comment 5, the overall comparison on the vary of temperatures seems be bit reliable. If it was applied on mask, the breath pressure should be listed as another parameter to compare? Some references on the mask or mask materials would be helpful, i.e. https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202102189; DOI: 10.1002/smll.202102903. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the helpful comment regarding breathing pressure and for directing us to the relevant mask-related references. We have carefully examined these works on advanced mask technologies and conducted additional experiments to clarify the influence of breathing pressure in our system. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on enhancing filtration efficiency or incorporating antimicrobial functionalities at the material level, our work aims to develop a multifunctional mask material that not only satisfies essential protective requirements but also enables integrated on-mask health monitoring 1, 2. We first conducted supplementary experiments using a ventilator simulator to mimic human breathing at different pressures while simultaneously monitoring voltage and resistance. We quantified the dynamic pressure generated by the breathing airflow. The results show that at ΔT = 0 K, neither the resistance nor the voltage exhibits any measurable change under varying breathing pressures (Fig. R3). This demonstrates that the mechanical pressure associated with breathing induces a negligible effect on the device’s resistance response, confirming that breath pressure has minimal influence on the output signal in our design. We further refined our analysis in the revised manuscript by updating Fig. 4b to include the quantified dynamic pressure during breathing (Fig. R4). The periodic voltage fluctuations closely track the temperature variations induced by breathing, while the corresponding dynamic pressure remains low and shows no correlation with the electrical output. This finding confirms that the device’s output is dominated by the thermal voltage generated from breath-induced temperature gradients, with negligible interference from airflow pressure. Consequently, the TEPUF-based mask can reliably monitor respiration even in challenging environments, without producing false signals arising from airflow or pressure fluctuations. Our modification to the manuscript: We have revised manuscript on Pages 17, 37 and Page 49 in the revised Supporting Information, with changes highlighted in blue.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents a three-dimensional (3D) multifunctional thermoelectric device technology consisting of porous polyurethane foam (PUF) coated with a waterproof conductive layer made from single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs), poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS), and waterborne polyurethane (WPU). The authors described that the Hydrogen bonding between the sulfonate groups in PEDOT:PSS and the -NH groups in WPU enhances water resistance (contact angle of 112°) and mechanical durability under repeated compression (20,000 cycles), maintaining a fast response time of 40 ms. The device has waterproof and signal-decoupling capabilities, it was demonstrated as an integrated underwater monitoring and interaction system. The concept sounds cute and fits to the journal scope well. The multifunctional sensing structure/patterned unit that can operate as a smart functioned HMI has been widely studied, but there are still more gaps to be bridged. But I have some reservations as showing below.
The top concern is that the Design and working mechanism of the Multi-modal monitoring system need be more explicit. The link between the design to the coupled effect seems very disconnected. Some references might be helpful to extend the scope (https://doi.org/10.1002/eom2.12448; https://doi.org/10.1002/eom2.12384).While the influencing factors have been discussed, the context need show analysis in the deformation and the associate geometrical factors in the region, to show the mechanical/thermal energy distribution. The mapping of critical dependent on the deployed location should be justified, the current evidence is confusing. The thermal/mechanical decoupling on the device systems deploy on inhaling mask and limb should be clearly highlighted. While the influencing factors have been discussed, the context didn’t show enough advantages in the control. Some results only contain limited data. I guess the contact mechanics should be presented here, some FEA data should be supplied to support the claim. The current details in Fig 3f seems far from enough. Moreover, the responding signal under certain pressure or load, seems never been justified under the proper geometrical area? The mechanics interpretation seems be largely missing in this work. Upon applying the load/pressure, how’s the interaction between layers, and energy dissipations? Please see the following references for the example details(https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202301117; https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202505048). The in-situ observation on the deformation of layer(s) should be interesting, to help the understandings.
There are also a few points for consideration:
1. The structural characterization and illustration are missing in Figures. How can we justify and creating the structure-property relationship without this?? The in-vivo validation seems be limited on the video, and less quantified. It hardly can say as convincing.
2. In Figure 2-3, the detailed mechanics analysis should be added, rather than only FEA. How the energy conversion rate? And energy loss in the multi-layer structure? The above discussion could be added to elaborate more on the result.
3. The logic in Fig 4-5 seems in adequate in terms of justify the operation of the proposed system, the demonstrations were incremental.
4. The technical details including surface/interface condition, the porous area during the deformation, which should be discussed. The degradation/failure of micro-structure can increase the deviation and lead to the inaccuracy of the output.
5. The writing and language in this manuscript also needs significant work. There are large chunky paragraphs and frequent language issues, which significantlt reduced the reading experience. I would recommend authors to revise and polish the context accordingly to a higher standard with an improved scientific interpretation.
Therefore, I would recommend to a rejection and transfer to a sister journal.

### Reviewer 2

The author proposed a three-dimensional thermoelectric foam (TEPUF) for underwater physiological signal monitoring for the first time, which possessed excellent waterproof performance, ultrahigh elasticity and dual-mode signal decoupling capability. The author systematically demonstrated the great potential of TEPUF in practical applications such as respiratory monitoring, body temperature recognition, swimming state recognition and gesture recognition. Further combining with sensor networks, machine learning algorithms and logic circuits, this work constructed an underwater early warning system, highlighting the practicality and innovation of this research. Overall, the manuscript is well-organized and will expand the application of thermoelectric materials and devices. Therefore, I strongly recommend that this work can be published in Nature Communications.
1. The manuscript reports that the Seebeck coefficient and resistance remain stable over 20,000 compression cycles (Fig. 2h), but the supporting information only provides resistance change data up to 2,000 cycles (Fig. S24). To ensure consistency and completeness, the authors should include resistance-change data for all 20,000 compression cycles.
2. Thermoelectric materials are also often used in wearable energy harvesting. It is suggested that the author supplement the data and tests related to energy harvesting.
3. The manuscript indicates that TEPUF has high air permeability and makes comparisons with other wearable multi-functional thermoelectric devices. It should be clearly stated whether these comparison devices were tested under the same pressure conditions.
4. It’s suggested to fully discuss the stability and adaptability of TEPUF under different water conditions.
5. The manuscript mentions the realization of multi-modal signal fusion and classification through machine learning algorithms, but the specific details and implementation process of the algorithms should be described in detail.

### Reviewer 3

The authors provide a multi‐modal underwater thermoelectric foam for wearable sensors. The thermoelectric foam not only has a water contact angle of 112°, a strain response of 40 ms, and a temperature resolution of 0.05K, but also has 408 mm s⁻¹ air permeability and 20000 times compression stability. The foam’s 3D porous structure enables efficient heat and moisture exchange while maintaining signal integrity underwater. The authors further integrate thermoelectric foam into underwater wearable devices for physiological parameter monitoring. The manuscript is well-structured and will expand the applications of thermoelectric devices in underwater environment. Therefore, I recommend this manuscript for publication after minor revisions.
1. The introduction appropriately emphasizes triboelectric nanogenerators in the context of self-powered sensors. However, it does not address other established self-powered mechanisms such as hydroelectric and piezoelectric technologies. A brief discussion of these alternatives would provide a more balanced overview and strengthen the contextual foundation of the manuscript.
2. Although the application of waterborne polyurethane (WPU) enhances circuit protection, the potential impact of excessive coating on the foam’s air permeability remains unaddressed. The authors should clarify how to control the prevent obstruction of the foam’s porous structure and ensure air permeability.
3. The manuscript introduces a underwater wearable monitoring system based on a distributed sensor network, yet it lacks a clear explanation of its innovative aspects. The authors should elaborate on the rationale behind employing an array-structured sensor system instead of miniaturized integrated units.
4. The test results (air permeability and water contact angle) were not accompanied by statistical analysis. To verify the reliability and repeatability of the research results, the author should include statistical indicators, such as standard deviation or error bars.
5. A key claim of the manuscript is the decoupling of multiple stimulus signals. However, the practical applications shown in Figures 4 and 5 do not clearly highlight the advancedness of such decoupling. The authors are encouraged to justify the relevance of signal decoupling in practical applications and provide corresponding evidence.

The author proposed a three-dimensional thermoelectric foam (TEPUF) for underwater physiological signal monitoring for the first time, which possessed excellent waterproof performance, ultrahigh elasticity and dual-mode signal decoupling capability. 1. The manuscript is well-structured and will expand the applications of thermoelectric devices in underwater environment. Therefore, I recommend this manuscript for publication after minor revisions.
1. The introduction appropriately emphasizes triboelectric nanogenerators in the context of self-powered sensors. However, it does not address other established self-powered mechanisms such as hydroelectric and piezoelectric technologies. A brief discussion of these alternatives would provide a more balanced overview and strengthen the contextual foundation of the manuscript.
2. Although the application of waterborne polyurethane (WPU) enhances circuit protection, the potential impact of excessive coating on the foam’s air permeability remains unaddressed. The authors should clarify how to control the prevent obstruction of the foam’s porous structure and ensure air permeability.
3. The manuscript introduces a underwater wearable monitoring system based on a distributed sensor network, yet it lacks a clear explanation of its innovative aspects. The authors should elaborate on the rationale behind employing an array-structured sensor system instead of miniaturized integrated units.
4. The test results (air permeability and water contact angle) were not accompanied by statistical analysis. To verify the reliability and repeatability of the research results, the author should include statistical indicators, such as standard deviation or error bars.
5. A key claim of the manuscript is the decoupling of multiple stimulus signals. However, the practical applications shown in Figures 4 and 5 do not clearly highlight the advancedness of such decoupling. The authors are encouraged to justify the relevance of signal decoupling in practical applications and provide corresponding evidence.

Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and the recommended references, which we have carefully reviewed to strengthen the theoretical foundation of our study. Wang et al. 9 reported a stratified, flexible gel composite in which energy dissipation is achieved through reversible, non-covalent interfacial interactions. Their soft multilayer structure features exceptionally tough interfaces and retains high durability after 10,000 cycles. Interlayer sliding was identified as the primary energy dissipation mechanism. In another work, Wang et al. 10 developed a dual-ion hydrogel network incorporating hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and polymer chain entanglement. This synergistic molecular design imparts high water retention, mechanical strength, and dynamic tunability, exemplifying effective molecular-level toughening and energy dissipation. In contrast, the TEPUF investigated in our study is a continuous foam that integrates elements of both mechanisms mentioned above. Its porous skeleton dissipates energy through intrinsic viscoelastic deformation and pore structure recovery. Unlike stratified systems, TEPUF lacks hierarchical interfaces, which eliminates the risk of interlayer delamination or failure. The coherent skeleton ensures robust mechanical support, while the uniform porous structure provides consistent performance and cyclic stability. These features collectively enable the device to maintain durability under prolonged cyclic loading. In repeated compression cycle tests, we observed a gradual reduction in the area of the stress–strain hysteresis loop for the TEPUF material, leading to a marked decrease in the energy loss coefficient after 20,000 cycles (Fig. R15). This suggests diminished energy dissipation during cyclic loading. The energy loss coefficient, defined as the ratio of dissipated energy to total input energy during a loading–unloading cycle, typically decreases as internal friction is reduced and elastic recovery improves. This behavior is consistent with the Mullins effect observed in polymer elastomers, where repeated deformation leads to rearrangement of polymer chains, resulting in decreased stiffness and hysteresis loss. In TEPUF, such adaptive microstructural reorganization likely occurs after initial cycles, enabling more reversible elastic deformation in subsequent loading. These findings suggest that TEPUF undergoes an initial “training” phase, after which it exhibits reduced mechanical loss, enhanced elasticity, and greater stability under long-term cyclic compression. Therefore, the decreasing hysteresis loss with increasing cycles highlights the material’s excellent mechanical durability and reversible deformation characteristics, supporting its suitability for applications involving repeated mechanical loading. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents a three-dimensional (3D) multifunctional thermoelectric device technology consisting of porous polyurethane foam (PUF) coated with a waterproof conductive layer made from single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs), poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS), and waterborne polyurethane (WPU). The authors described that the Hydrogen bonding between the sulfonate groups in PEDOT:PSS and the -NH groups in WPU enhances water resistance (contact angle of 112°) and mechanical durability under repeated compression (20,000 cycles), maintaining a fast response time of 40 ms. The device has waterproof and signal-decoupling capabilities, it was demonstrated as an integrated underwater monitoring and interaction system. The concept sounds cute and fits to the journal scope well. The multifunctional sensing structure/patterned unit that can operate as a smart functioned HMI has been widely studied, but there are still more gaps to be bridged. But I have some reservations as showing below.
The top concern is that the Design and working mechanism of the Multi-modal monitoring system need be more explicit. The link between the design to the coupled effect seems very disconnected. Some references might be helpful to extend the scope (https://doi.org/10.1002/eom2.12448; https://doi.org/10.1002/eom2.12384).While the influencing factors have been discussed, the context need show analysis in the deformation and the associate geometrical factors in the region, to show the mechanical/thermal energy distribution. The mapping of critical dependent on the deployed location should be justified, the current evidence is confusing. The thermal/mechanical decoupling on the device systems deploy on inhaling mask and limb should be clearly highlighted. While the influencing factors have been discussed, the context didn’t show enough advantages in the control. Some results only contain limited data. I guess the contact mechanics should be presented here, some FEA data should be supplied to support the claim. The current details in Fig 3f seems far from enough. Moreover, the responding signal under certain pressure or load, seems never been justified under the proper geometrical area? The mechanics interpretation seems be largely missing in this work. Upon applying the load/pressure, how’s the interaction between layers, and energy dissipations? Please see the following references for the example details(https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202301117; https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202505048). The in-situ observation on the deformation of layer(s) should be interesting, to help the understandings.
There are also a few points for consideration:
1. The structural characterization and illustration are missing in Figures. How can we justify and creating the structure-property relationship without this?? The in-vivo validation seems be limited on the video, and less quantified. It hardly can say as convincing.
2. In Figure 2-3, the detailed mechanics analysis should be added, rather than only FEA. How the energy conversion rate? And energy loss in the multi-layer structure? The above discussion could be added to elaborate more on the result.
3. The logic in Fig 4-5 seems in adequate in terms of justify the operation of the proposed system, the demonstrations were incremental.
4. The technical details including surface/interface condition, the porous area during the deformation, which should be discussed. The degradation/failure of micro-structure can increase the deviation and lead to the inaccuracy of the output.
5. The writing and language in this manuscript also needs significant work. There are large chunky paragraphs and frequent language issues, which significantlt reduced the reading experience. I would recommend authors to revise and polish the context accordingly to a higher standard with an improved scientific interpretation.
Therefore, I would recommend to a rejection and transfer to a sister journal.

### Reviewer 2

The author proposed a three-dimensional thermoelectric foam (TEPUF) for underwater physiological signal monitoring for the first time, which possessed excellent waterproof performance, ultrahigh elasticity and dual-mode signal decoupling capability. The author systematically demonstrated the great potential of TEPUF in practical applications such as respiratory monitoring, body temperature recognition, swimming state recognition and gesture recognition. Further combining with sensor networks, machine learning algorithms and logic circuits, this work constructed an underwater early warning system, highlighting the practicality and innovation of this research. Overall, the manuscript is well-organized and will expand the application of thermoelectric materials and devices. Therefore, I strongly recommend that this work can be published in Nature Communications.
1. The manuscript reports that the Seebeck coefficient and resistance remain stable over 20,000 compression cycles (Fig. 2h), but the supporting information only provides resistance change data up to 2,000 cycles (Fig. S24). To ensure consistency and completeness, the authors should include resistance-change data for all 20,000 compression cycles.
2. Thermoelectric materials are also often used in wearable energy harvesting. It is suggested that the author supplement the data and tests related to energy harvesting.
3. The manuscript indicates that TEPUF has high air permeability and makes comparisons with other wearable multi-functional thermoelectric devices. It should be clearly stated whether these comparison devices were tested under the same pressure conditions.
4. It’s suggested to fully discuss the stability and adaptability of TEPUF under different water conditions.
5. The manuscript mentions the realization of multi-modal signal fusion and classification through machine learning algorithms, but the specific details and implementation process of the algorithms should be described in detail.

### Reviewer 3

The authors provide a multi‐modal underwater thermoelectric foam for wearable sensors. The thermoelectric foam not only has a water contact angle of 112°, a strain response of 40 ms, and a temperature resolution of 0.05K, but also has 408 mm s⁻¹ air permeability and 20000 times compression stability. The foam’s 3D porous structure enables efficient heat and moisture exchange while maintaining signal integrity underwater. The authors further integrate thermoelectric foam into underwater wearable devices for physiological parameter monitoring. The manuscript is well-structured and will expand the applications of thermoelectric devices in underwater environment. Therefore, I recommend this manuscript for publication after minor revisions.
1. The introduction appropriately emphasizes triboelectric nanogenerators in the context of self-powered sensors. However, it does not address other established self-powered mechanisms such as hydroelectric and piezoelectric technologies. A brief discussion of these alternatives would provide a more balanced overview and strengthen the contextual foundation of the manuscript.
2. Although the application of waterborne polyurethane (WPU) enhances circuit protection, the potential impact of excessive coating on the foam’s air permeability remains unaddressed. The authors should clarify how to control the prevent obstruction of the foam’s porous structure and ensure air permeability.
3. The manuscript introduces a underwater wearable monitoring system based on a distributed sensor network, yet it lacks a clear explanation of its innovative aspects. The authors should elaborate on the rationale behind employing an array-structured sensor system instead of miniaturized integrated units.
4. The test results (air permeability and water contact angle) were not accompanied by statistical analysis. To verify the reliability and repeatability of the research results, the author should include statistical indicators, such as standard deviation or error bars.
5. A key claim of the manuscript is the decoupling of multiple stimulus signals. However, the practical applications shown in Figures 4 and 5 do not clearly highlight the advancedness of such decoupling. The authors are encouraged to justify the relevance of signal decoupling in practical applications and provide corresponding evidence.

Comment 7: The mechanics interpretation seems be largely missing in this work. Upon applying the load/pressure, how’s the interaction between layers, and energy dissipations? Please see the following references for the example details (https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202301117; https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202505048). Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and the recommended references, which we have carefully reviewed to strengthen the theoretical foundation of our study. Wang et al. 9 reported a stratified, flexible gel composite in which energy dissipation is achieved through reversible, non-covalent interfacial interactions. Their soft multilayer structure features exceptionally tough interfaces and retains high durability after 10,000 cycles. Interlayer sliding was identified as the primary energy dissipation mechanism. In another work, Wang et al. 10 developed a dual-ion hydrogel network incorporating hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and polymer chain entanglement. This synergistic molecular design imparts high water retention, mechanical strength, and dynamic tunability, exemplifying effective molecular-level toughening and energy dissipation. In contrast, the TEPUF investigated in our study is a continuous foam that integrates elements of both mechanisms mentioned above. Its porous skeleton dissipates energy through intrinsic viscoelastic deformation and pore structure recovery. Unlike stratified systems, TEPUF lacks hierarchical interfaces, which eliminates the risk of interlayer delamination or failure. The coherent skeleton ensures robust mechanical support, while the uniform porous structure provides consistent performance and cyclic stability. These features collectively enable the device to maintain durability under prolonged cyclic loading. In repeated compression cycle tests, we observed a gradual reduction in the area of the stress–strain hysteresis loop for the TEPUF material, leading to a marked decrease in the energy loss coefficient after 20,000 cycles (Fig. R15). This suggests diminished energy dissipation during cyclic loading. The energy loss coefficient, defined as the ratio of dissipated energy to total input energy during a loading–unloading cycle, typically decreases as internal friction is reduced and elastic recovery improves. This behavior is consistent with the Mullins effect observed in polymer elastomers, where repeated deformation leads to rearrangement of polymer chains, resulting in decreased stiffness and hysteresis loss. In TEPUF, such adaptive microstructural reorganization likely occurs after initial cycles, enabling more reversible elastic deformation in subsequent loading. These findings suggest that TEPUF undergoes an initial “training” phase, after which it exhibits reduced mechanical loss, enhanced elasticity, and greater stability under long-term cyclic compression. Therefore, the decreasing hysteresis loss with increasing cycles highlights the material’s excellent mechanical durability and reversible deformation characteristics, supporting its suitability for applications involving repeated mechanical loading. The inter-pore spacing decreases slightly but remains uniform, suggesting a homogeneous compression response. At 40% strain (Fig. R16e), pores further flatten into oblate or polygonal shapes, and the framework becomes significantly denser. Increased wall curvature and early signs of wrinkling are seen (Fig. R16f), though no cracking is observed, highlighting the material’s excellent damage tolerance. The strain is primarily absorbed through wall buckling, with uniform pore shrinkage and stable global structure. At 60% strain (Fig. R16g), pores are highly compressed, and inter-skeletal spacing is further reduced. Wall buckling and intersecting wrinkles become more prominent (Fig. R16h), forming a compact but crack-free network. At 80% strain (Fig. R16i), the structure approaches its compression limit, and the skeleton height is significantly minimized. Severe wall bending, folding, and localized undulations appear (Fig. R16j), yet no large-scale fractures or collapse occur. Energy dissipation at this stage is primarily governed by wall buckling, with visible crease marks but maintained structural integrity. After complete unloading, the structure nearly returns to its original geometry. Figs. R16k and R16l show that the skeleton height and morphology are almost fully recovered, with pores reopening and only minor residual bending. This is expected for open-cell foams like TEPUF, where the interconnected polymer skeleton bears the mechanical load, and the voids serve merely as structural space without contributing to stress transmission. The simulated stress distribution highlights pronounced stress concentrations at skeletal junctions and curved regions, while most pore spaces exhibit minimal stress (Fig. R2). These results align with established understanding of porous materials, where mechanical performance is largely governed by the composition and geometry of the skeletal framework. Our findings confirm that TEPUF’s mechanical strength is determined primarily by the architecture of its skeleton. Geometric factors such as pore wall thickness and connectivity dictate how stress propagates through the network. When properly engineered, the skeleton distributes stress uniformly, minimizing localized concentrations and enhancing overall mechanical resilience. The FEA results clearly illustrate TEPUF’s characteristic load-bearing porous architecture, in which the solid frame is the principal stress carrier. This structural design explains its stability and resistance to collapse under compressive loads, supporting its suitability for demanding, cyclic mechanical environments. Comment 5: The manuscript mentions the realization of multi-modal signal fusion and classification through machine learning algorithms, but the specific details and implementation process of the algorithms should be described in detail. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. To achieve effective fusion and classification of heterogeneous multi-modal signals, we have implemented a machine learning framework based on support vector machines (SVM), incorporating feature standardization, kernel function selection, and hyperparameter optimization. The original multi-modal signals were first aligned and structured into a unified two-dimensional feature matrix. To eliminate numerical scale differences among features from different modalities, z-score standardization was applied, ensuring numerical stability and improving convergence efficiency during model training. For model construction, the radial basis function (RBF) kernel was chosen due to its strong capability in handling non-linear classification problems. To identify the optimal model configuration, we performed 5-fold cross-validation combined with a grid search across a predefined parameter space, allowing us to select the best-performing hyperparameter combination for the SVM classifier. Comment 1: The introduction appropriately emphasizes triboelectric nanogenerators in the context of self-powered sensors. However, it does not address other established self-powered mechanisms such as hydroelectric and piezoelectric technologies. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. As noted, while our introduction emphasized triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) as underwater self-powered sensors, it provided limited discussion of other mechanisms such as hydroelectric and piezoelectric technologies. Recent studies have indeed explored hydroelectric harvesters and piezoelectric transducers for underwater sensing and wearable applications. For example, Zhang et al. developed a flexible piezo-acoustic patch capable of sensing, positioning, and underwater wireless communication 11, which successfully monitored divers’ heart rates and transmitted the data acoustically. However, such technologies present notable limitations for underwater wearable applications. They often rely on rigid components, suffer from reduced stability under prolonged immersion, and are challenging to integrate into flexible, skin-conformable platforms. Furthermore, the majority of existing research on underwater self-powered sensing still predominantly focuses on TENGs. As discussed in our manuscript, TENG-based systems typically require bulky encapsulation that compromises comfort and flexibility, and most support only single-mode sensing. In contrast, our TEPUF device was specifically designed to overcome these limitations. It offers multi-modal signal decoupling, intrinsic waterproofing without the need for external encapsulation, and improved wearability, providing a more practical and versatile solution for underwater self-powered sensing applications. Comment 2: Although the application of waterborne polyurethane (WPU) enhances circuit protection, the potential impact of excessive coating on the foam’s air permeability remains unaddressed. The authors should clarify how to control the prevent obstruction of the foam’s porous structure and ensure air permeability. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. This issue is indeed critical, as air permeability and water resistance in foam materials are typically inversely related, and achieving an optimal balance between these properties remains a core challenge in materials design. To address this, we conducted supplementary experiments to evaluate the effect of coating composition on performance. We prepared PUF samples with WPU:SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS mass ratios of 0:2, 1:2, and 2:2, and measured air permeability using a YG461G tester. As shown in Fig. R25, the uncoated sample (0:2) exhibits high air permeability (527 mm s−1 at 100 Pa), but its hydrophilic surface readily absorbs water, making it unsuitable for underwater or humid environments. In contrast, the 2:2 coating significantly enhances waterproofing but suppresses air permeability to just 9.97 mm s−1, which compromises comfort and usability. To further correlate waterproofing with coating composition, we measured water contact angles (Fig. R26). The 0:2 sample shows a contact angle of ~88.7°, confirming its hydrophilicity and poor water resistance. The 2:2 sample exhibits a contact angle of ~129°, indicating strong hydrophobicity but at the cost of reduced permeability. Notably, the 1:2 coated sample achieves a balanced performance, with a water contact angle of ~112° and high air permeability (406 mm s−1), indicating effective waterproofing while maintaining breathability. To assess long-term protection, we subjected the samples to 8 hours of continuous water washing and monitored resistance changes (Fig. R27). The uncoated sample showed a significant resistance drop due to water ingress and degradation of the conductive network. In contrast, the 1:2 coated sample maintained stable conductivity, with negligible resistance change, demonstrating effective protection. While the 2:2 sample also preserved conductivity, its low air permeability limits its practicality for wearable applications. Overall, the 1:2 WPU:SWCNTs/PEDOT:PSS coating offers the optimal trade-off between breathability, waterproofing, and long-term stability, making it the most suitable choice for wearable use. Comment 3: The manuscript introduces a underwater wearable monitoring system based on a distributed sensor network, yet it lacks a clear explanation of its innovative aspects. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. We fully acknowledge the issues raised and would like to further clarify the innovations and advantages of the proposed sensor array architecture. Underwater physiological monitoring involves multiple parameters, such as temperature, breathing rate, and motion, which are challenging to capture simultaneously and accurately with a single-site or monolithic device. Our distributed sensor array addresses this limitation by allowing individual TEPUF units to be strategically positioned at critical locations, such as joints, inside diving masks, or on the chest. This proximity to the signal sources significantly enhances measurement accuracy and signal stability. The array consists of nine TEPUF elements connected in series, with each unit independently capable of sensing both temperature and pressure. The series configuration enables the summation of individual element voltages, thereby substantially increasing the overall output signal (Fig. R28). Additionally, the spatial distribution allows the array to collect data from multiple body regions or external heat sources, facilitating multipoint sensing and higher signal amplitude. Moreover, distributing the sensing load across multiple elements enhances response stability and improves wearer comfort by reducing localized pressure. Overall, this architecture not only supports multifunctional and high-fidelity sensing but also offers practical advantages in wearable underwater applications. Comment 5: A key claim of the manuscript is the decoupling of multiple stimulus signals. However, the practical applications shown in Figures 4 and 5 do not clearly highlight the advancedness of such decoupling. The authors are encouraged to justify the relevance of signal decoupling in practical applications and provide corresponding evidence. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. Multi-modal signal decoupling is indeed critical for accurate underwater monitoring. In practical application scenarios, temperature variations and pressure signals often occur simultaneously, for example, body surface temperature changes during swimming, airflow temperature fluctuations during breathing, and pressure shifts from gesture-induced joint movement. Without effective decoupling, the system may misinterpret temperature changes as pressure signals, or confuse motion stimuli with thermal responses, leading to recognition errors and functional cross-talk that significantly compromise monitoring accuracy. In gesture recognition or respiratory monitoring, for instance, body movement or joint compression can alter local temperature, potentially triggering false alerts if signals are not clearly separated. Similarly, temperature fluctuations caused by exhaled breath could be mistakenly interpreted as grip force or motion, further emphasizing the importance of robust signal decoupling to ensure reliable and accurate physiological sensing in dynamic underwater environments. The TEPUF designed in this work strategically leverages the distinct response characteristics of its material structure and underlying physical mechanisms to achieve natural signal decoupling. Experimental results demonstrate that under a constant temperature difference, varying the applied pressure yields a stable pressure–resistance response curve, while the thermoelectric voltage remains virtually unaffected. Conversely, when the temperature difference increases under constant pressure, the thermoelectric voltage rises linearly with temperature, while the resistance remains unchanged (Fig. R31). This independent response behavior confirms the decoupling of the thermoelectric and piezoresistive effects in TEPUF. Such decoupling prevents signal interference and significantly improves measurement accuracy. For example, in respiratory monitoring experiments, periodic fluctuations in thermal voltage corresponding to breathing cycles were observed, while the strain resistance remained stable (Fig. R8 on page 8 of this response letter). Similarly, during underwater limb monitoring, resistance changes were clearly recorded during motion, whereas the thermoelectric voltage remained constant, indicating that mechanical disturbances do not affect thermal gradient measurements (Fig. R10 on page 9 of this response letter). These findings confirm that TEPUF can effectively separate thermal and mechanical signals in complex, dynamic environments. Furthermore, the multi-modal safety system illustrated in Fig. 5 utilizes decoupled inputs, temperature, motion, and breathing, for integrated analysis and real-time early warning. Thus, signal decoupling is central to the system’s reliability, stability, and sensing accuracy.
